#3264. IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

#3259. The Best Last-Minute Gifts That Don't Feel Last Minute

This series will help you pick the perfect presents, decor, and activities to make this Christmas the Best Christmas Ever.

We’ve all experienced gift panic—that sinking feeling when you realize you need a present in an hour and you just don’t have one to give. Whether you spent all year chasing the “perfect” gift or simply procrastinated, your time is nearly up. But don’t panic. The clock may have nearly run out, but your options haven’t. Before you resort to re-gifting something from the back of a closet, here’s how to pull off a last-minute gift that is effortless but feels elevated and worthy of the person you’re giving it to.

With the right presentation, even the most last-minute gift can read as thoughtful. Any performer will tell you that the difference between a good show and a bad one comes down to commitment and confidence. The same is true for last-minute gifts: If you act like your gift is thoughtful and intentional, they’ll think it is. The biggest mistake people make is apologizing as they hand over a present—nothing ruins a vibe faster than, “Sorry this is so last-minute.” So give with confidence.

And focus on presentation. A handwritten note that contains a shared memory or personal joke can elevate a present. Use simple but personal wrapping; craft paper and twine, or a reusable gift bag that looks like you planned ahead. Add a small flourish, like a sprig of holly or a fancy bow. Small touches can make it seem like you’ve carefully prepared. What you don’t want are obvious panic gifts that scream, “I grabbed this on the way here.” The goal is effortless, not frantic.

Digital gifts are your friends. You can order something in minutes that arrives instantly online, and with a little thought, will still read as personal and intentional. The trick is choosing a present that speaks to the recipient’s tastes, hobbies, or quirks, and pairing it with a small note to show you remember what they love. From e-books to streaming subscriptions, these gifts hit the sweet spot of thoughtful and last-minute. Here are some suggestion:

When time is running out, gift cards are your secret weapon. They arrive instantly online, don’t require shipping, and with the right presentation, they can feel surprisingly thoughtful. The key is to pick a card that fits the recipient’s interests and add a personal note. The more specific you are, the better. If your giftee is into Italian food, get them an Eataly gift card. If they're a PC gamer, get them a Steam card. If they're into education, a membership to Skillshare is perfect. There's a gift card out there for just about any interest, and all you have to do it google it and email it.

Generic gift cards can be a last-minute lifesaver that can still seem a little personal if you give them the right way.

Pick a theme or design: Many online cards, like Amazon, Etsy, or Starbucks, let you choose designs. The right visual makes the card feel more intentional.

Include a warm, personal message: Even one line can make a digital card feel thoughtful—something like, “I couldn’t pick just one thing for you. Hope this helps you treat yourself.”

Send strategically: Deliver the card by email or text, but consider printing the email or screenshotting it in a small envelope so it feels like a “real” gift.

Sign someone up for a subscription service, write a note explaining you want to keep giving them presents all year, and you're golden. Here are some suggestions:

SnackCrate: This service sends a different snack from around the world every month.

SpiceClub: For the culinary adventurer on your list. A subscription to RawSpiceBar’s Spice Club delivers a curated selection of spices every month.

Mocktail Club: Booze-free fancy drinks delivered once a month? Sign me up.

Thera Box: If you know someone in need of some self-care, this once-a-month box is packed with wellness and relaxation items.

Loot Crate: If your giftee is geeky, consider this monthly surprise box of pop culture treasures.

Cameo is a platform where celebrities, influencers, musicians, and performers create personalized video messages for fans. If someone on your list is a fan of someone on Cameo, you can set up a session, and give a card with a mysterious note like "Keep an eye out for a special message." They'll be delighted with a personal message from wrestling legend Mick Foley or terrified when Chris Hansen appears on their screen; your choice.

I have enough crap in my house, so I love getting experiences instead of things. The challenge with experience gifts is usually timing: Many require reservations or coordination, but there are plenty of options that let your giftee schedule the time, making them perfect last-minute gifts.

Museum membership cards: Many institutions sell digital gift memberships that the recipient can activate whenever they like.

Movie tickets: Your local multiplex probably has a gift certificate you can buy online.

Local attraction passes: Some city attractions offer gift cards or “anytime admission” tickets that don’t expire immediately.

Pair these with a note explaining why you chose the experience, or, if you have that kind of relationship, something like, "I want to take you to the Museum of Modern Art." Just make sure you follow through and actually go.

Sometimes, there’s literally no time to order, wrap, or even think about a gift. If you’re scrambling out the door and need something now, you might be able to fake your way through, even if you're stopping at the liquor store on the way to the Christmas party.

Flowers or a small potted plant: Give a seasonal bouquet or a small indoor plant. Add a handwritten note, even a single line, and it might come off as thoughtful.

Gourmet chocolates or candy: Specialty chocolates from a local shop or grocery store display can feel luxe with a little ribbon or bag.

Wine, craft beer, or non-alcoholic beverage: A bottle with a clean label or interesting packaging immediately elevates your gift. Ask the clerk at the liquor store to help you find something unique.

Lottery tickets: Who wouldn't appreciate a bunch of scratch-off lottery tickets?

Hard cash is the most impersonal gift of all, but the only one you know will be used. This gift really depends on the person getting it, so be aware of whether they're likely to think "Just what I wanted!" or "Wait, I'm not poor." If you give cash, make sure it's crisp bills in a nice card, with a personalized note.

#3257. Stephen Wilson Jr.’s Month Just Got Even Bigger Thanks to U2

Stephen Wilson Jr. is having one remarkable month. The genre-blurring singer-guitarist received his first-ever Grammy nominations on Nov. 16 and quickly followed up the milestone two days later when, at 47 years old, he was named New Artist of the Year at the 60th CMA Awards.

But arguably his most high-profile recognition came just this Tuesday, when U2 revealed dates for the U.S. leg of their Greatest Show on Earth Tour: Wilson will open nine of the band’s 15 announced stadium shows. (The War on Drugs will handle the six others.)

The direct-support slot for one of the most anticipated tours of 2027 should introduce the Indiana native to a whole new audience, one that may not already know him for his indie-rock style of country music (what Wilson calls “Death Cab for Country”), his viral cover of Ben E. King’s “Stand by Me,” or the video of his quotable CMA acceptance speech that’s been making the rounds online. “I learned that the mining is the real gold,” Wilson said onstage.

Wilson’s appearance on U2’s tour also reinforces his burgeoning rock cred. In September, he performed Temple of the Dog’s “Hunger Strike” with Eddie Vedder at Vedder’s curated Ohana Fest. And earlier this month, he put his own spin on “Wonderwall” to help honor Oasis at their Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony in L.A. It’s not a stretch to say that Wilson has more in common sonically with rock — or even grunge — than he does Nashville country music.

“I’m very much an indie rock kid at heart. That’s where I cut my teeth, as a player, as a performer, as an artist,” he once told Rolling Stone. “But I’m a country songwriter. Wilson is set to follow up his 2023 double-album debut, Son of Dad, with another ambitious double LP, Impression of a Human // Children of the Cornerman. Set for release on Feb. 26, the album features both of Wilson’s Grammy-nominated songs: “Hardwired” with Miranda Lambert, and “Gary,” his celebration of the working class. The latter half of its title, Children of the Cornerman, nods to the boxing that shaped his youth and remains a part of his routine.

He made sure to acknowledge the sweet science during his CMAs speech. “My first stage was a boxing ring,” Wilson said, explaining how it taught him to handle pressure — perhaps the kind he’ll face onstage next summer in front of his biggest concert audiences yet. Apple made a bunch of changes to iOS to optimize it for the iPhone Duo’s form factor, including revamping the Lock Screen. According to a new leak today, the company has tested another change, referred to as a “complication column.” Here’s what it looks like.

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

On the iPhone Duo’s Lock Screen right now, you can add widgets along the bottom of the interface. On the bottom right, you have two controls that default to the flashlight and camera. You can customize these and link them to other controls from Apple and third-party apps.

Cellular and Wi-Fi information is located along the top right-hand side of the iPhone Duo’s Lock Screen.

According to the spelunking account pdfu on X, Apple has tested a “complication column” that would appear along the right edge of the Lock Screen. The column has room for two widgets, filling the space between the flashlight/camera controls and the Wi-Fi and cellular status icons. These widgets are the same size as the widgets that appear along the bottom.

The “complication column” for iPhone Duo was first spotted in iOS 27.1 code, the account says. No code changes have been made since, so it’s unclear whether the feature is still in active development or Apple has scrapped it.

Apple has tested a “complication column” for iPhone Duo’s Lock Screen. It fits two circular widgets along the right edge.Flag: SpringBoard/Ionic (disabled). First seen in iOS 27.1, with no code changes since. pic.twitter.com/orjOuvM1Xs

I hope this “complication column” idea is still in development and makes it into a future iOS 27 update. What about you? Let us know down in the comments.

#3254. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.)

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue

Tereza Pultarova is a London-based journalist specializing in aerospace and defense technologies. She is a native of the Czech Republic.

I enjoyed this piece very, very much, and I truly hope this team continues its work.

Those are some pretty impressive photos! It also seems like the iron ion filtering is pretty unique. I love seeing cases where people build something they want to see in the world with minimal outside support. Seems like it would be a solid return on more public money to seek out and support scrappy projects like this one.

Looking for a coffee machine to see you through all twelve months of the year (and then some)? The Smeg Espresso & Cold Brew Machine might just scratch that itch. This aesthetically pleasing machine can make genuinely cold cold brew — no lukewarm extraction here — and delicious, hot espresso. Although it's quite expensive in the U.S., it could be an ideal first machine for the budding enthusiast.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

What do you look for when shopping for an espresso machine? Function? Coffee-snob-approved features? Affordability? Or style? If it’s the latter, may I introduce you to the Smeg ECF03 — one of the most aesthetically pleasing espresso machines I’ve ever seen?

Also called the Smeg Espresso & Cold Brew Machine, the ECF03 combines Smeg’s trademark ‘50s design with some seriously impressive functionality. The machine makes genuinely cold cold brew — not lukewarm like De’Longhi — and delicious espresso. While the steam wand takes a while to heat up and requires some patience for back-to-back shots, it’s a fun little machine for newbies.

However, its MSRP isn’t a fun little price tag for newbies — in the U.S., it’ll set you back $699. In the U.K. you can grab it for as low as £204. No, that’s not a typo. £204. So, is this enough to make it one of the best espresso machines? To find out, you’ll need to keep reading this Smeg ECF03 review.

Single shot portafilter (single-walled and dual-walled), double shot portafilter (single-walled and dual-walled), tamper, cleaning disc, brush, cleaning needle

The Smeg ECF03 is outrageously expensive in the U.S., and pretty par for the course in the U.K. On the east side of the Atlantic, you’re looking at $699 from Amazon, but over on the west, you’ll only pay £399 at John Lewis. It’s also on clearance at Curry’s for £204, which is utterly bizarre, seeing as this machine only came out last year, but I’d recommend buying there if you’re fast. I’m not sure how long that sale price will last as I write this.

In the U.S., this machine is really overpriced. $699 for a Thermoblock espresso machine with no grinder is steep. For $699, you can get the Breville Barista Express or the Breville Bambino Plus with the Baratza Encore ESP grinder.

You can also get the De’Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo for $699, which has a built-in grinder, and the Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini for $449 — which also has a built-in grinder.

See what I mean? You’d still have to buy a grinder separately to make the most of the ECF03. That’s an extra $200. An MSRP of around $400-$500 would have made more sense, putting the ECF03 in line with the best entry-level espresso machines, Breville Bambino Plus and Breville Bambino ($299).

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Of course, the ECF03 can make cold brew, so you wouldn’t need to purchase a separate cold brew maker or French press for cold brew, but I’m not sure this is worth the extra $200-$300 over Breville’s options. On top of that, the aforementioned De’Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo can make “cold brew” for the same price.

I use quotation marks because De’Longhi’s cold brew comes out warm — but I’ll get into that later.

While the ECF03 has a 58mm portafilter — closer to the specialty coffee commercial standard than Breville’s 54mm — I’m not sure that’s worth the extra $$$.

The ECF03 looks like (almost) everything Smeg makes: retro, stylish, and oh-so cool. The only machine to forgo the trademark Smeg aesthetic is the $1,599 Semi-Professional/Mini Pro/EMC02 (the many-monikered machine), which was a collaboration between Smeg and La Pavoni.

If you like the Smeg aesthetic, you’ll be pleased. If it’s not your cup of tea, you won’t be pleased. It’s as simple as that.

For a $699 machine, though, the ECF03 is a touch more plasticky than I’d like. That gorgeous white chassis? Shiny plastic. The steam wand knob also feels like plastic. If it’s not actually plastic, color me surprised, but it sure does look and feel like it.

There’s a manometer, which is a nice touch, but it doesn’t actually show the specific bar pressure of each step. I assume anything in the perforated section on the bottom right means over 9 bars, but I’d like numbers on the next iteration of this machine.

But the accessories. Oh, the accessories. They’re beautiful. The 58mm tamper is super weighty, making it feel incredibly high quality, and the 58mm portafilter is just as professional. They actually feel like weapons. This is the mark of a high-quality machine. If you unbox a $500+ espresso machine and the tamper is plastic, run. Run fast.

Naturally, you get a pressurized (dual-wall) and non-pressurized (single-wall) portafilter basket. I only used the single-wall one as I have the best grinder in the world, Mazzer Philos, so I didn’t need to resort to the help-I’ve-used-pre-ground-coffee-and-now-my-espresso-tastes-bad dual-walled portafilters.

The Smeg ECF03 makes delicious espresso. As mentioned earlier, I used the non-pressurized portafilters and fresh Ethiopian beans ground on my Mazzer Philos. I recommend you also use freshly ground coffee and the non-pressurized portafilters for the best experience. Pressurized portafilters can destroy nuance and delicate flavors in specialty coffee beans, but are fine for pre-ground coffee if that’s what you like.

To make espresso, I ground 18g of my Ethiopian coffee beans to click 25 on the Philos, which is coarser than the Fellow Espresso Series 1’s ($1,499) optimal grind size, but similar to the Breville Bambino’s ideal range of 22-25. For context, I use the same coffee beans for every single machine.

Here’s a photo of a “perfect” espresso. This extracted 35.6g in 26 seconds, which is in the “golden window” of espresso extraction.

As you can see, there’s a lovely crema on top, with a delicate, fluffy texture and a nice color to the shot. While this might not impress serious espresso enthusiasts — the shot was a little bitter at the end of the mouthful — it’s definitely fine if you are less of a hobbyist and more of an appreciator.

Overall, the espresso tastes very Italian. Strong-bodied, rich, and dark, even when using medium-roasted beans. Again, if you’re an espresso enthusiast, you might want to invest a little more in the Fellow Espresso Series 1 or Lelit Mara X3 ($1,999) — or the Smeg EMC02, which I still dream about.

As an integral part of this machine’s marketing, it’s only logical I discuss cold brew in detail. You access cold brew via the “Blue menu”, which is activated by pressing the power button while the machine is already switched on. The buttons will glow blue, meaning you’re in cold brew mode.

According to the manual, you’re supposed to use “one or two” ice cubes per cold brew, but I ignored that. I filled my cup about halfway with ice cubes, dosed 18g of medium-fine ground coffee in the non-pressurized portafilter basket, and set it to pull a double shot of cold brew. Not sure how you can get a “double shot” of cold brew, but I assume that’s just the machine’s limited button options.

The cold brew took four minutes and fifty-three seconds to fill my glass. The machine is programmed to dose a certain volume of cold brew, but I used a 12-ounce glass filled with ice, so I didn’t need the “whole” serving.

As you can see, it’s relatively dark, with a strong body. The ice cubes aren’t all melted — can you guess what that means? Yes, it actually brews cold! This is fantastic news; De’Longhi machines tend to brew lukewarm, or sometimes even actively warm cold brew (which then requires ice to make it cold).

As for the taste, this cold brew was fine. I wouldn’t throw away my Espro P7 French press, which I use to make cold brew the traditional way (16 hours at room temperature), but I also wouldn’t turn my nose up at rapid cold brew from the Smeg. I think this will do if you want a cold coffee in a pinch, but serious cold brew lovers need not apply.

While the ECF03 makes a delicious espresso, its steam wand isn’t as powerful as I’d like it to be. Don’t get me wrong, this is nowhere near as egregious as machines like the Casabrews Ultra ($349), but for $699, I’d expect at least a Bambino Plus-level wand.

I was able to get perfect microfoam, but it took a while to steam an 8oz jug — around a minute. Here’s a photo of a flat white I made on the ECF03.

As you can see, the milk texture is perfect, with smooth, almost melted-marshmallow texture. There are zero bubbles and the milk is extremely creamy. This tasted divine.

However, it’s worth noting that I’m an ex-professional barista and an espresso machine tester of almost three years. I have a lot of practice. If this is your first espresso machine, you will need to baby that steam wand. Because it’s lower pressure than the Breville Bambino/Bambino Plus, you’ll need to learn how to eke out delicate texture even when you can’t achieve the perfect vortex.

At 14.3 x 8.1 x 11.6 inches, the ECF03 isn’t the smallest, nor the largest, espresso machine I’ve tested. As it has no grinder, you’ll need a separate one, so I recommend making sure you’ve got enough to room for both the machine and its grinder before purchasing.

The water tank is at the back of the machine, so you’ll need a decent amount of upper-cupboard clearance space — at least 17 inches, I’d say.

Speaking of water tank, Smeg provides you with water hardness strips, but no water filter. If you wanted to filter your water, you’d need to buy that separately. Smeg sells these for $25 on its website, which is pretty disappointing to see considering this machine is already $699.

When you do need to descale, Smeg doesn’t sell its own descaler. I’d recommend using De’Longhi’s or Durgol’s, which are $19 for 2 bottles and $15 for 4 bottles, respectively.

Last but certainly not least — warranty. Smeg offers a 2-year warranty if purchased from the Smeg store or a 1-year warranty from another outlet. This is pretty disappointing when De’Longhi, Breville, and Ninja all offer 2-year warranties as standard — and many of their machines cost less than the ECF03.

The Smeg ECF03 is ideal for espresso beginners. If you want to feel fancier than, say, a Casabrews (and you have the money to back it up, of course), then by all means you should invest in a Smeg. The ECF03 is really easy to use, makes actually cold cold brew, and has a mostly useful manometer for pressure-watching.

Although the steam wand means you need to really pay attention during milk heating, if you’re willing to put the work in, you’ll get barista-quality coffee out of it. And I mean… just look at it! Everything Smeg makes is an aesthetic marvel, and the ECF03 is no different.

If you’re in the U.K., you’re getting a much better deal, but if you find it on sale in the U.S., I’m sure you won’t be disappointed.

Erin Bashford is a senior writer at Tom's Guide. She has a Master's in Broadcast and Digital Journalism from the University of East Anglia. She directs Tom's Guide's dedicated coffee video series, The Coffee Lab, which you can find on all social media channels. On top of her passion for coffee, she's a huge music nerd and is most often found wearing earbuds or headphones — or blasting music from her multi-room sound system. When she's not writing about lifestyle culture at Tom's Guide, she's probably reading a fantasy novel, writing a fantasy novel, playing The Sims, practising yoga, or hiking.

iOS 27 includes a really clever new feature that aims to solve the awkward middle ground between cellular and Wi-Fi connectivity. Here’s how it works and how you can turn it on.

In a support document, Apple explains that Connectivity Assist uses cellular data to improve your connection when Wi-Fi is slow or unusable. Apple uses examples like your backyard or driveway, as well as “coffee shops, airports, sports venues, and everywhere in between.”

Essentially, the feature detects when your Wi-Fi connection is weak or unusable and intelligently uses cellular data to keep you connected.

One practical example I’ve noticed is when I walk out of my house and get in my car. Oftentimes, my iPhone will cling to my house’s weak Wi-Fi connection, making it hard to start playing Apple Music and queue up directions in Apple Maps.

Connectivity Assist solves that problem. My phone can now intelligently use cellular data to help that transition away from Wi-Fi. It’s one of many really nice quality-of-life improvements in iOS 27.

You can turn Connectivity Assist on or off with these steps:

Another thing to be aware of is that you might use more cellular data with Connectivity Assist turned on. You can monitor your data usage via your carrier’s app or website, as well as in the Settings app on iPhone.

#3250. The Country Song About Losing Your Virginity That Became an Enduring Hit

A song about getting ditched for a Texas woman might be leading the charts right now, but, 30 years ago, Deana Carter was offering a different take on romance: the enduring, nostalgic ache of that first love. Or, if we’re being a little less polite, losing your virginity to a college guy next to a river.

The Matraca Berg and Gary Harrison-written hit “Strawberry Wine” went to Number One on country radio in November 1996, and was a seminal part of a female-dominated wave where the genre’s women could push the boundaries of what exactly they were singing about, and how they were singing it. It still resonates.

A softly-delivered ballad, “Strawberry Wine” wasn’t as outwardly bold as songs like Loretta Lynn’s “Rated X,” or deeply topical like Dolly Parton’s “Down From Dover.” Instead, it’s a wistful reflection on a teen girl’s first love, with a hair of melancholy — and how thinking back on pangs of pleasure can hit as deep in the gut as a good country song. Carter never specifically details exactly what happened between her and this summer fling, but it’s pretty clear what she’s talking about: “love growin’ wild,” “the loss of my innocence,” intoxication, being plucked from the vine before entirely ripening.

As the first single from her album with the equally boundary pushing title Did I Shave My Legs for This, Carter offered a quiet, cheeky reclamation of how subtly or overtly women could sing about sex. And not just sex: sex that comes before, and has nothing to do with, marriage or domestic life, completely devoid of the male gaze.

Carter was 30 when “Strawberry Wine” became a hit, later in life as far as the industry standards for women generally go. A Nashville native, she grew up around music through the eyes of her father, guitarist Fred Carter Jr., who appeared on records by Bob Dylan, Simon & Garfunkel, and Willie Nelson. Carter wrote most of the songs on her debut, but found that “Strawberry Wine” “just nailed my life story, which ended up being everyone’s first experience [with love],” she said in an interview for CMA’s ‘90s Country Forever. She was particularly drawn to the work of Berg, one of the genre’s strongest and boldest talents, unafraid to pitch songs about female experiences to women willing to sing them. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

And Carter was the only one open to taking that risk. Artists like Trisha Yearwood, among many others, reportedly passed on “Strawberry Wine.” But Carter was willing to give a ballad about youthful carnality a go.

“It’s a five-minute waltz about… ya know,” Berg told Rolling Stone. “Deana was a brand-new artist and she wanted it as her first single. That shocked me. She was a friend of mine, so I was trying to talk her out of it because I wanted her to do well.” Shockingly enough, it did: the song hit Number One at country radio, a rarity for ballad sung by a woman, and went on to inspire others like Kelsea Ballerini, Elizabeth Cook, Ashley McBryde, and Mickey Guyton, who even shouted out “Strawberry Wine” in her song “Rosé” (so did Kid Rock, but we don’t need to mention that one).

Cook, who was motivated to pursue music thanks to Carter’s songs, also referenced it in “Two Chords and a Lie.” “She knows the words to ‘Strawberry Wine’ / It’s a friendly reminder of how love is blind,” Cook sings, in one of dozens of country songs that call out Carter’s hit. Trending Stories Cher’s Victory in Royalties War Under Fire as Mary Bono Pushes for Reversal Chris Christie to Republicans: ‘I Don’t Want to Hear Your Whining’ Amanda Seyfried Admits She ‘Told a Lot of People’ About Elizabeth Holmes Documentary 50 Years Ago Today: Neil Young Played a 1 A.M. Concert the Morning of the Last Waltz

These days, country has been racier than ever. From Kacey Musgraves’ washing machine, to Lainey Wilson’s steamy new single “Just a Woman,” the influence of Carter and “Strawberry Wine” holds strong. Wilson even once recorded a mashup of her very “Strawberry Wine- inspired “Watermelon Moonshine” on social media, the two hits intertwining.

“I was definitely channeling ‘Strawberry Wine.’ There will never be another one, but this is kind of my version of that,” Wilson told Variety. “I think songs like that, that are nostalgic like that, they’re just timeless. People can relate. They want to go back to that place; everybody wants to feel at home.”

#3249. The Best Tech Deals From the Sam's Club Early Black Friday Sale

Retailers and brands are churning out early Black Friday deals already, including the likes of Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, Samsung, and others. If you're waiting around for Friday, Nov. 27 to do all of your shopping, you might miss out on some deals and unnecessarily make the day more stressful than it needs to be. If you're a Sam's Club member, you have access to many early Black Friday deals worth checking out. I spent some time combing through their website and rounded up my favorite tech deals below.

The Bose SoundLink Flex SE is a portable Bluetooth speaker with an IP67 waterproof rating. The speaker even floats in the water, so you can bring it with you into the pool. While it doesn't offer full EQ customization in its companion app, the sound has rich bass depth and clear highs out of the box. It also features a speakerphone, allowing you to take calls and speak with it. It's light and portable, and the Bluetooth 5.3 supports multipoint connectivity and SBC, AAC, and aptX codecs. You can get the Bose 2nd Generation SoundLink Flex SE for $89 (originally $139).

Skullcandy makes fun speakers and headphones, although they're not designed for audiophiles (their sound signature is very bass-heavy). Their Skullcandy Stomp XL Max is their attempt at making a portable party speaker. It comes with two wireless mics, making it a great option for karaoke. It holds 12 hours of battery life (up to 20 hours with certain settings), has an IPX5 water resistance rating, and has LED lights that sync to the music. You can get it for $99 (originally $199).

Getting a soundbar can exponentially improve anyone's entertainment system, but a 5.1 system with rear speakers and a subwoofer takes it to the next level. The Samsung HW-Q65F 5.1 Channel Soundbar is $299 (originally $399), and it's a wireless setup that will keep the harmony of "too many cables" in the house. It supports Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X to give you a 3D audio feel, and it has a dialogue feature that will let you hear the whispers.

These kinds of sales are always a good time to upgrade laptops. If you're looking for a powerful computer that is well-rounded, consider the 16-inch HP OmniBook 7 Flip going for $699 (originally $899). This laptop comes with an Intel Ultra 5 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 16GB of RAM (which, honestly, is the minimum anyone should be buying in 2026).

If you need a bigger screen, the 17.3-inch HP OmniBook 3 is a good choice for a bit less money at $649 (originally $999). It comes with an Intel Core Ultra 7 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 12GB of RAM. Part of the bigger screen means a bigger keyboard, so if you deal with numbers a lot, you'd likely appreciate the numeric pad.

If you want your laptop strictly for gaming, the ASUS TUF F16 Gaming laptop is $1,149 (originally $1,399). With an Intel Core 7 processor and the RTX 5060 graphics card, you'll be well set up to tackle heavy games. It comes with a 165Hz refresh rate, Advanced Arc Flow fans and vents to keep your machine cool, and 16GB DDR5 RAM to keep your loads short.

Gaming monitors can get expensive quickly, but you can get decent options on a budget. A great example is the 31.5-inch MSi gaming monitor selling for $129 (originally $179). It has a 250Hz refresh rate and a 1ms response time to make gaming smoother. There's also AMD FreeSync Premium to get rid of tearing and stuttering.

Budget TVs get big discounts during Black Friday, and the 58-inch Vizio QLED TV is one of them. You can get one for $178 (originally $298), and it supports Dolby Vision HDR for better color and contrast. The operating system is the Vizio OS, but of course, you can always change it with a TV dongle if you prefer a different one.

If you prefer to splurge for a better QLED but still get a good deal, the 65-inch Samsung QN90H QLED TV at $1,197.99 (originally $1,497.99) is a great option. It upscales lower-resolution pictures to 4K with AI. It works for gaming with its 144Hz refresh rate, and because the operating system is Tizen OS, it comes with Samsung TV Plus, which brings over 2,700 free channels. The TV also comes with Dolby Atmos, so you can hear audio with a 3D effect as the audio follows objects around the display.

A 100-inch TV makes a statement: You take your entertainment system seriously. The 100-inch Vizio QLED TV is a budget-friendly option with a $300 discount, currently going for $1,198 (originally $1,498). This TV supports Dolby Vision HDR for more vivid images and has hundreds of free channels with the Vizio OS.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Sam Club's 2026 Black Friday sale runs from November 26 to November 29, 2026, starting online at 12:01 a.m. on Thanksgiving Day, but the deals start even earlier.

Yes, you'll need to be a member to get the deals, but you can shop online without a membership with a 10% surcharge. However, you can always get a year membership for $120, which includes a Walmart+ membership, free shipping, and other perks.

Sam's Club seems to have more TV deals than Walmart, but Walmart usually has the best deals for budget TVs. Depending on what you're looking for, one might be better than the other.

#3248. Five recent tech outages were not due to AI; the next round will be

Five major tech outages in quick succession earlier this month led to speculation that they were connected, with some inevitably believing them to be AI-related.

That wasn’t the case, but the US Director of National Intelligence is one of a number of experts warning that we should expect AI-powered outages in the near future …

Earlier this month saw five tech outages, one after the other. A widespread Microsoft 365 outage occurred when two unrelated issues coincided. The next day saw a nationwide ground stop of US air traffic due to a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centers. A few days later, a bug in a Chase bank system saw disruption not only to the bank itself, but also other banks where Chase was a party to a transaction. Many Apple services went offline later the same week, with retail stores also affected. Finally, United Airlines had its own widespread IT outage that grounded a significant number of flights.

Each had their own unrelated causes, with the White House stating that rumors of an AI-facilitated systemic attack by a hostile state were false.

However, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has warned that we should expect future tech outages as a result of attacks facilitated by AI-discovered vulnerabilities. CNBC reports him issuing the warning on CNN’s State of the Union.

The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.

You prepare by knowing that systems are going to be upgraded; they may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and government are dealing with this on the front foot.

We already saw an example of this last month when a vulnerability discovered in PHP saw a significant number of websites being taken offline.

Microsoft President Brad Smith says it isn’t just a question of bad actors exploiting vulnerabilities discovered by AI, but companies rushing to patch these may inadvertently cause systems to fail, as Newsweek reports.

What AI did earlier this year was basically make it much easier for people to find vulnerabilities in code, and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you’re a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems.

Especially when you have older infrastructure, especially when you’re trying to patch at such a pace, especially when you have to go so fast that you can’t take as much time to test what you’re changing in the code, you do increase the risk of something going wrong.

Major IT failures look set to be a routine event in the coming weeks and months.

#3246. As Apple works on AI agent features, banks are already blocking them

One of the most dramatic shifts in the AI landscape is the emergence of intelligent agents that can use iPhone and Mac apps in order to carry out tasks on our behalf.

We can already use third-party chatbots in this way, and we know Apple is working hard to turn Siri AI into an agent. However, before the company even gets the chance, banks are already blocking them, and this may be just the start …

The science fiction promise of AI has always been to be able to tell a computer what we want done and have the task carried out for us automatically. That’s starting to turn into a reality with the emergence of AI agents.

We’ve already seen Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, and Muse gain agent capabilities, and Apple is expected to bring these to Siri AI at some point next year.

Earlier this month, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said that the company ultimately wants to go in this direction and may add these abilities next year. CEO John Ternus has reportedly been pushing Craig Federighi for faster software development, with specific mention of “moving beyond necessary improvements to Siri,” which seems likely to mean agentic capabilities.

Last week also saw a since-deleted Apple job listing detailing plans for autonomous AI agents.

We’ve already seen some of the ways in which this can go wrong, and we recently outlined three significant risks. Wired reports that banks are now responding to these by either blocking AI agents or warning customers that using them can be dangerous.

JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with your credentials. That same day, Bank of America warned its customers not to share login info with agents. Along with the announced change coming from Wells Fargo, Citibank and PNC have also changed their terms to include warnings about agents.

Wells Fargo even goes as far as using capitals in its latest terms, stating that it will not be responsible for the consequences.

Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK

We can likely expect similar pushback in sectors like online shopping as companies fear high returns costs and other consequences from mistakes by AI agents.

Personally, I don’t give any AI agents access to any of my banking or other financial services, considering the risks to be too high. I don’t see my position changing any time soon.

What’s your take? Would you trust an AI agent with access to your bank accounts? If not, would Apple launching agentic capabilities for Siri AI change your view? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3244. Use Your Year-End Review to Reach for a Promotion

Maintaining a document of your successes throughout the year gives you a starting point

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech).

That plan stalled my career for about five years.

I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role.

So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?”

I took the counteroffer and stayed. Three jobs in, I finally got promoted, and all it took was asking (in the most dramatic way possible).

Today, I would take a different approach.

Year-end review discussions are a great time to push for a promotion. But at most companies, raises and promotions are largely settled before the formal review conversation happens. If the year-end review is the first time your manager hears you want a promotion, you’re usually too late.

Now is a great time to start the conversation.

Engineers tend to believe good work speaks for itself. It rarely does. Your manager is juggling a team, a roadmap, and their own boss. They see a fraction of what you do, and the work they don’t see might as well not exist when raises get decided.

Perception is reality, so you have to shape it. That means learning to brag a little.

A “brag document” is a running list of what you accomplished, when, and why it mattered. Add to it every two weeks or once a month, and write each entry so your manager’s manager would understand it.

Engineers tend to write things like “migrated the billing service.” A better entry reads “migrated the billing service, which cut failed payments by 30 percent and unblocked the Q3 pricing launch.” If there’s no number, name who benefited and how.

Include the work people forget to count, too: handling incidents, mentoring new hires, interviewing candidates, and writing the docs everyone else relies on. If you helped your team adopt AI tools this year, write that down. (It counts as leadership, whether or not anyone called it that.)

The document does two jobs. It gives you ammunition when you make your case, and it gives your manager something to ctrl + c then ctrl + v when they argue for you in meetings you’ll never attend.

Bragging builds the case. Asking forces action.

If your goal is a promotion or a raise, you might ask: “What would it take for me to get to [the next level] in the next year?”

A good manager will give you an outline that can turn into a plan. Push for specifics until you have deliverables you can work toward, then send a short recap email so the plan exists somewhere besides your manager’s memory. (Managers change jobs too.)

Sometimes the answer will still be “not this year,” and the reason may have nothing to do with you.

Budgets get frozen, promotion slots get capped, and decisions get made above your manager’s head where even a manager who wants to help can’t.

Don’t read too much into that. But be honest with yourself, too. Most of the time, a no means there’s something you aren’t doing yet. Find out what it is instead of guessing for five years like I did.

Asking costs you one slightly awkward conversation. Sitting back and waiting to be noticed can cost you years.

Don’t try this at home: To better understand the risk AI slop poses to scientific publishing today, IEEE Spectrum contributor Benjamin Skuse put IEEE’s research integrity checks to the test by submitting two entirely AI-generated papers. “Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up…”

Policy change doesn’t just come down to paid lobbyists—lawmakers want to hear from working experts, too. One engineer shares what he learned from his first two visits to Capitol Hill.

Could community colleges help fill the coming talent shortage in the U.S. semiconductor industry? Alternatives to four-year university degrees are a promising option for the technicians who will be needed to run new fabs.

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, an online education platform that helps people break into AI and modern software roles through project-based learning and one-on-one mentorship with senior developers. #3242. ‘All of a Sudden’ Is the Rare Movie That May Change Your Life

We go to the movies for any number of reasons: to laugh, to cry, to care (bless you, Nicole Kidman), to be thrilled or scared or see if Spider-Man makes it out of a scrape with a supervillain alive. The notion that we might be drawn to films so we can listen to other people talk — to be not just voyeurs but eavesdroppers — isn’t usually one of the top reasons for spending a lot of time sitting in the dark and staring at shadows on a screen. It’s a show-don’t-tell medium.

Still, there are a handful of auteurs who excel at making the art of conversation seem everything from enthralling to downright cinematic. Tarantino loves letting his characters digress at length in between violent set pieces and gratuitous shots of feet. The work of French writer-director Eric Rohmer is synonymous with long sequences of people doing nothing more than chatting about intellectual matters great and small. (His work also gave us one of the all-time great 1970’s cine-disses.) If Louis Malle had made nothing but My Dinner With Andre, he’d still be considered canon-worthy. Richard Linklater, Jean Eustache, Whit Stillman — all first-rate movie conversationalists. And then there’s Ryusuke Hamaguchi.

As anyone who’s seen the Oscar winner Drive My Car and Happy Hour — his 2015 magnum opus that clocks in at a little over five hours, and frankly could have sustained itself for twice that running time — will tell you, the Japanese filmmaker can take extended scenes of discussion and turn them into the sort of exchanges that make you lean forward. If anyone could make a connect-the-dots presentation about capitalism, healthcare, and burnout cycles scrawled onto a whiteboard in real time feel absolutely compelling, it’s him. That happens to be the centerpiece of his latest drama All of a Sudden, an ironic title for a masterwork intent on taking its time and giving its characters plenty of space to ruminate. The end result is all the better for it, too. This is the type of movie that prizes philosophical pursuits over pulse-pounding chases, and the spark of communicating ideas over crass spectacle. It’s admittedly not for everyone. For filmgoers who find two human beings connecting over reflections on life, death, art, and caretaking, however, Hamaguchi’s astounding ode to empathy as an emotional foundation for coexistence is nothing short of manna. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

The person giving that impromptu whiteboard lecture is Mari (Tao Okomoto), a Japanese playwright and theater director who’s mounting one of her productions in Paris. The woman on the receiving end of this Socio-economics 101 lesson is Marie-Lou (Virginia Efira). She is the director of a memory-care facility, overseeing a half-dozen or so patients. Marie-Lou is a staunch advocate for “humanitude,” a four-pillar methodology developed in France for treating those enduring various stages of dementia and Alzheimer’s. (Hamaguchi himself became familiar with this technique when his grandmother was being cared for roughly a decade ago.) The younger members of her staff are slow to adapt to this ideology that emphasizes touch and “verticality” over more traditional treatment plans; the older nurses are flat out refusing to learn it at all. The uphill battle of fighting for what is, in Marie-Lou’s eyes, a more humane way of healthcare is taking its toll on her.

It’s pure coincidence that Marie-Lou happens to meet Mari after an encounter with a developmentally disabled kid (Kodai Kurasaki) and his grandfather (Kyôzô Nagatsuka), who happens to be an actor in Mari’s play. The two hit it off, and after a performance, hang out and talk, talk, talk through the wee small hours. By the time we witness Marie-Lou being schooling on how the world works via whiteboard, you can tell the bond between these two is tight. Lifelong friendships have been forged over less.

Hamaguchi is using a 2019 collection of letters between Maho Isono and Makiko Miyano, known in some English editions as You and I: The Illness Got Worse, as a foundation here — which makes All of a Sudden something like an adaptation, and the equivalent of an epistolary movie. Correspondence is king here; it just happens to be occurring face to face instead of one post at a time. Like Isano, Marie-Lou comes from a medical background. And like Miyano, a philosopher by trade, Mari has a tendency to think big thoughts and emphasize the way that the “littlest” people make up (and are at the mercy of) a far bigger picture. It’s worth noting Miyano was diagnosed with terminal cancer when she met her pen pal — a condition that Hamaguchi passes on to Mari as well. Time is something that seems to contract, expand, and often feel like it stops still in the director’s work. But in terms of Mari and Marie-Lou’s story, it’s very much of the essence. Their time together is fleeting, and the last thing they’re taking for granted. Related Content She Cries. She Rages. She Sings Harry Styles. Is Sandra Hüller the MVP of 2026? It Was Butchered Beyond Belief. Now the Most Shocking 1970s Movie Returns as a Masterpiece Taylor Swift to Perform at Academy Museum's Annual Gala ‘NAZA’ Wants You to Bear Witness

All of a Sudden is filled with languorous side trips, large chunks of stand-alone bits of business, and segments centered around caretaking that almost feel like process movies unto themselves. A performance of Mari’s play is essentially seen in full, then partially reprised near the end. Training sessions and testimonials from family members and loved ones of patients share screen time with our central duo’s chatathons. Anyone squeamish over the idea of a group foot massage (part of the humanitude’s more experimental notions of engagement between facility workers and their wards) may want to leave for popcorn before the film hits its three-hour mark. Mari wants to return to Japan to deal with her illness, so Marie-Lou goes with her. So does the movie. Trending Stories Cher’s Victory in Royalties War Under Fire as Mary Bono Pushes for Reversal Chris Christie to Republicans: ‘I Don’t Want to Hear Your Whining’ Amanda Seyfried Admits She ‘Told a Lot of People’ About Elizabeth Holmes Documentary 50 Years Ago Today: Neil Young Played a 1 A.M. Concert the Morning of the Last Waltz

Yet Hamaguchi’s not simply letting seemingly tangential events or the daily drudge of work luxuriously play out for their own sake. Every minute is accounted for story-wise, and not a moment is wasted. He’s not painting a portrait so much as a mural, one that keeps its central duo in constant focus even as its generous with its supporting players and peripheral bits of business. We should note that both Efira and Okomoto are equally outstanding, solo and in tandem, and equally adept at holding up their ends of the long conversations that punctuate the filmmaker’s meditations on how one spends what little time they have on this hurling rock in the cosmos. There’s a rapport happening between the two that bypasses cultural backgrounds, different performing styles, separate languages — the dialogue moves back and forth between French and Japanese so fluently that it sometimes takes you a second to realize when switches between tongues. The lingua franca here is a shared understanding of the need for companionship and the joy of communication. Not for nothing did both of them share the Best Actress award at Cannes.

It’s thrilling to watch what is, at its base, an origin story of a friendship, even if we know it’s a brief one — because we know where this ends. Yet Hamaguchi wants to acknowledge that quality, not quantity, is what matters in terms of togetherness. That applies to the humanism that underlines every thing that’s on screen as well, and that particular quality is in abundance. The movie may seem to drift, to detour, or to determinedly test one’s patience when examining things outside of Mari and Marie-Lou’s rich discussions about the world they live in, and the world they’ll leave behind. Yet All of a Sudden is all of a piece, and makes listening in feel like an honor. Hamaguchi is delivering an eloquent statement about the need for looking after one another in a myriad of different ways, ranging from creativity to giving someone a good farewell. Despite keeping one eye on death, it’s a primer for a possible way to live a good life — and the rare movie that may change yours.
