Black Friday is always the day after Thanksgiving. This year, Black Friday starts at midnight on Nov. 27. Cyber Monday is the Monday following Black Friday, which starts at midnight on Nov. 30.

The major retailers running sales are the usual ones: Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Home Depot, and many others. Currently, Walmart has publicized its plans already and has early deals available. Best Buy is offering one of the largest Black Friday and Cyber Week sales, with multiple events and early deals. Target has a three-day event. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

Unlike Spring or Summer sales, Black Friday doesn't focus on specific categories, which means everything is fair game for discounts. #3219. Bob Seger Mourns ‘Extraordinary’ Silver Bullet Band Bassist Chris Campbell

Earlier this week, Silver Bullet Band bassist Chris Campbell, who played alongside Bob Seger from 1969 through his final tour in 2019, died of natural causes at 78. Tributes poured in from across the music world, and now Seger himself has weighed in.

“With the passing of our bassist and my friend for over 55 years, Chris Campbell, it’s taken me a couple of days to put my thoughts together, such a huge and sad loss,” Seger wrote in a statement. “Chris was with us as we started out traveling to gigs in station wagons and vans and for the next forty plus years - all the way through our last show in 2019.

“He was a great musician,” Seger continued. “Chris understood well the roots of rock and roll, rhythm and blues.  His ability to lock into a pocket with a drummer was extraordinary and he was remarkably consistent show to show.  Off stage, his sense of humor kept us laughing and entertained.  Chris was like family; we raised our kids together.  It was a blessing to share this journey with Chris, and I’ll cherish the memories forever.  RIP my friend.”

Campbell joined the Bob Seger System in 1969, just one year after “Ramblin’ Gamblin’ Man” became their first nationwide hit. “I was hired in what I thought was a temporary job as bass player because Dan Honaker had just broken his wrist about a week before the Mongrel tour [in a motorcycle accident],” Campbell told Rolling Stone in 2011. “I had a week to prepare. I had to learn this album frontwards and backwards.”

The Bob Seger System dissolved a few years later, but Seger kept Campbell in mind when he formed a new group not long afterwards. “He said, ‘I’m thinking of putting a band together,'” Campbell told Rolling Stone. “I said to him, ‘That’s kind of bizarre, I have a keyboard player and a drummer.’ He goes, ‘I got a guitarist, Drew Abbott.’ That was the start of the Silver Bullet Band.”

Many members came and went from the Silver Bullet Band over the years, but Campbell was a constant, playing on many of Seger’s biggest hits, including “Night Moves,” “Turn the Page,” “Against the Wind,” and “Still the Same.”  Trending Stories Cher’s Victory in Royalties War Under Fire as Mary Bono Pushes for Reversal Chris Christie to Republicans: ‘I Don’t Want to Hear Your Whining’ Amanda Seyfried Admits She ‘Told a Lot of People’ About Elizabeth Holmes Documentary 50 Years Ago Today: Neil Young Played a 1 A.M. Concert the Morning of the Last Waltz

“This is my life, and I’m very happy with it,” Campbell told Rolling Stone. “I have wonderful kids and a good life, and we’re all friends. We’re all very fortunate. There’s no animosity and no fighting. Bob is our rock, our patriarch. We all look up to him. He’s so easy to work with. He’s a wonderful man, just as a human being.”

A couple years after a farewell tour ended in 2019, Campbell sued Seger over alleged unpaid royalty and touring payments. The majority of the case was ultimately thrown out by a judge.

Amazon is offering early Black Friday discounts on like-new versions of its 2024 Kindles, with prices starting at $161.99 for the Paperwhite Signature Edition. The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $161.99 from $224.99, almost 30% off. For that price, you're doubling the storage of a standard Paperwhite and getting wireless charging, an ad-free lock screen, and a front light that automatically adjusts to your surroundings—on top of the same sharp seven-inch display, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life as the standard Paperwhite, as noted by this PCMag review.

Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

#3211. Apple has three products coming next year that I’m very excited for

Apple is wrapping up a packed year for new products, but there are already several 2027 launches I’m very excited for. Here are my current most anticipated new products rumored for next year.

The iPhone’s 20th anniversary is rumored to bring a special new model that’s been dubbed ‘iPhone 20 Pro.’

iPhone 20 Pro is expected to introduce a new design inspired by the iPhone Air, reintroducing curves and possibly titanium, and with a quad-curved display that wraps around the edges for a bezel-free appearance.

I recently decided the iPhone Duo wasn’t the right model for me. While I’ll certainly be interested to see how the device evolves in its second generation, I’m far more excited for the iPhone 20 Pro as a fresh iteration on slab phones. Combining the strengths of a Pro model (cameras, battery) with the design traits of iPhone Air sounds very compelling.

I’ve been using Apple’s HomeView a lot since getting one earlier this month. And despite some Siri hiccups likely tied to the iOS 27.3 beta, I’m overall really loving the product and my family is too.

Because HomeView has been a hit for us, I’m eager to see how Apple evolves and expands it with the rumored ‘HomeView Ultra’ with a 9-inch screen that can automatically rotate 360° to face whoever’s speaking.

I have no complaints about the current HomeView’s size, but am intrigued by a larger screen’s impact on the overall experience. Mostly though, the idea of a HomeView that automatically rotates to face you sounds really useful. There’s a spot in my kitchen that would be perfect for kitchen and dining room use if the screen could swivel automatically.

The Apple Watch Series 13 might introduce an overhauled design, with one leaker claiming it will break compatibility of watch bands.

I’m tempering my expectations for this, since plenty of Apple Watch redesign rumors have come and gone with little actual change. But Mark Gurman has hinted we might get a redesigned Watch next year too. And after years of the same basic look, I’m fascinated to see what the next generation of Apple Watch design could be.

I’m very happy with my Apple Watch Series 12, and it’s becoming even more powerful with watchOS 27.3. But it’s very much an update focused on internals, so if Apple does deliver an external overhaul, the new Watch will merit its spot among my most anticipated products list.

Samsung’s flagship soundbars have reached the point where the yearly upgrades are more about refinement than reinvention, and that is pretty much the story with the Samsung HW-Q990H—and this 2026 model is on sale for $500 off for Black Friday, down to $1,497.99 from $1,997.99. That's its lowest price to date.

Samsung kept the same 11.1.4-channel setup from the older HW-Q990F, including the soundbar, wireless subwoofer, and two rear speakers, but leaned harder into software this time around—features like the SpaceFit Sound Pro automatically adjust the sound depending on your room layout, and unlike some auto-calibration features that barely change anything, this one reportedly shifts the audio balance in noticeable ways. Sometimes it improves dialogue clarity and bass response. Other times, you may prefer tweaking things yourself with the built-in seven-band EQ.

The system also handles basically every major audio format, supports wireless Dolby Atmos with compatible Samsung TVs, and includes 4K 120Hz HDMI passthrough for people gaming on a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X. That said, while the bass is strong for a compact subwoofer, it compresses when you push the volume near maximum, so it's not perfect for huge spaces or people who want nightclub-level output. More importantly, if you already own the HW-Q990F or even the older HW-Q990D, upgrading probably will not feel dramatic enough to justify the cost. But for someone starting from TV speakers or an entry-level soundbar, this system can completely change how movies, games, and even sports feel at home.

#3206. iOS 27 gave your iPhone an alarm feature that’s long been missing

Alarms are one of the most important iPhone features, and iOS 27 offers a key feature that should help your alarm actually wake you: a new volume setting for alarms that’s independent of other volume settings.

Have you ever accidentally slept through an alarm? We’ve all done it. And most often for me, it’s because my alarm volume was unintentionally set to a very low level.

I suspect that’s a pretty common reason for missed alarms. And in iOS 27, Apple finally has the fix—but it requires manually setting up.

Inside Settings ⇾ Sounds & Haptics, you can now set a volume for alarms that’s independent from the systemwide ringtone setting.

iOS 27 has two new sections in this Settings screen: Alarms and Timers, and Alerts and System Sounds. Both include ‘Match Ringtone Volume’ toggles that are on by default. This means your volume for alarms, timers, alerts, and other system sounds are all determined by the ringtone volume.

But if you disable the Alarms and Timers toggle, you’ll get a new volume slider that applies only to those system functions, and won’t be impacted by your ringtone volume.

As seen above, this means you can crank the Alarms and Timers volume up to the maximum level without making every other system sound, including notifications and phone calls, be similarly deafening.

So the next time you sleep through your alarm, it won’t be because the alarm was too quiet.

In case you missed it, iOS 26 introduced a welcome feature that lets you set custom snooze durations for alarms, and also an option to have alarms trigger on your iPhone even if you’re wearing an Apple Watch.

Do you plan to set a custom volume setting for alarms in iOS 27? Let us know in the comments.

#3201. MagSafe Monday: Anker’s MagGo Pro 2 has a built-in fan to keep 25W Qi2.2 charging from slowing down

The biggest issue with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat. It doesn’t matter if the battery specs say it can charge at Qi2.2 speeds if the heat slows it down after 15 minutes. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro directly targets heat with a built-in fan in the MagSafe battery.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge. Anker’s answer in the MagGo 2 Pro is a small fan inside of it. Anker says it keeps the charging surface below 96.8°F, and the fan adjusts its speed based on what’s plugged in and how the charge is progressing. You can switch between Cool and Silent modes if you don’t want to hear it running at all.

The result of having this fan is a Qi2.2 power bank that actually reaches Qi2.2 speeds for a full charge. Anker rates it at 25% on an iPhone 17 Pro in 10 minutes, then to 50% in 25 minutes, which is the kind of speed you’d normally expect from a wired charging session.

The MagGo 2 Pro battery is 10,000mAh, which is enough for a little over one full charge of an iPhone Pro Max and closer to two on a standard iPhone. Size-wise, it has about the same footprint as the iPhone itself and is roughly an ounce lighter than Anker’s standard MagGo. It’s not a slim battery, but for one with a fan, it’s workable in your travel bag, crossbody, etc.

The single USB-C port works both directions at up to 45 watts. If you plug in a 45-watt charger to it, the MagGo 2 Pro can charge from empty to 80% in under an hour. The same port will charge a Mac or an iPad up to 45 watts in a pinch, which is a nice add-on for a MagSafe battery. You are not going to charge up your MacBook Pro from zero to full with it, but it’s a nice way to get a little charge in an emergency at the airport, etc.

One thing to know before you buy: the cable in the box is a 1-foot USB-C-to-USB-C cable, and Anker says that reaching the full 45-watt recharge speed requires a 45-watt-rated cable. So keep that in mind as you pack for a trip.

Anker put a small display on the side that cycles through six screens with a side button: charging wattage, battery percentage, battery health, and temperature. It’s a nice touch to know you are reaching the 25-watt Qi 2.2 speed.

There’s also a built-in stand that adjusts from flat to 80 degrees and folds back into the body when you’re done. You can also quickly turn off charging if you simply want to use it as a stand. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro comes in Phantom Gray, Burgundy Red, Polar Night Blue, and Starlight Silver.

Qi2.2 is the Holy Grail of MagSafe chargers, but as I said in the beginning, it’s irrelevant if the heat throttles it. To get full 25-watt MagSafe charging on the go, you’ll likely need something with a fan, unless you’re in colder weather. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro solves that problem with a built-in fan, a handy side display, and a stand.

The Anker MagGo 2 Pro is available on Amazon and directly from Anker.

#3200. Jane Fonda, Robert De Niro & Other Figures Sign Letter Backing Chris Van Hollen For Majority Leader — Amid A Chuck Schumer Aide’s Prank

Jane Fonda, Robert De Niro and Chelsea Handler are among the entertainment figures who have signed on to a letter backing Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) in his bid to become Senate majority leader over Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-NY).

The letter, signed by about three dozen figures describing themselves as donors, fundraisers and artists, stated that in this year’s midterms, “voters delivered not on ly a mandate but an opportunity for change: a government that delivers real value in the daily lives of working families.”

“That change will only come from renewed leadership with a vision for the future,” the letter stated. “The Democratic Party has a trust and credibility problem, and fixing it requires Senate leaders willing to challenge the entrenched interests and power structures that protect those in power, in both parties.” The letter also called on senators to support candidates “who are dedicated to accountability, transparency and the bold agenda voters demanded.” Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Al Gore To Purchase Hometown Paper Carthage Courier News MS NOW Hosts Sign On To Letter Urging Adoption Of "Fair" WGAE Contract; Network Says Talks Are Ongoing And "Constructive"

The election for majority leader, to be held early next month, has highlighted party divisions, including among donors and in the entertainment industry, and even after the whopping victories of Democrats across the country in the midterms.

Noting that the upcoming vote on a Senate leader will be chosen by secret ballot, the letter called on the caucus to support Van Hollen, who is challenging Schumer, the current minority leader who had been the presumptive favorite to win following Democrats huge gains in which they flipped control of the chamber.

Others who signed on to the letter include Bruce Cohen, Padma Lakshmi, Laurie David, David Mandel, Fisher Stevens, Marisa Tomei, Amy Ziering and Morgan Spector.

In a statement. De Niro said, “Americans voted for the change necessary to fight the corruption, cruelty, and policies of Trump and his Epstein class cronies. That’s why I’m supporting change in Senate leadership. Chris Van Hollen is a progressive leader and a fierce fighter. He’s the right person to lead the Senate majority.”

Van Hollen has pitched his candidacy as a necessary response to the midterm results and that Democrats’ unexpected gains were also calls for change, coming from the left and the middle of the party.

“The voters responsible for the Blue Tsunami want fundamental change and bold, new ideas. Simply put, Chuck Schumer is the past and Chris Van Hollen is the present and the future,” Cohen said.

Schumer has insisted that he will emerge victorious, and even some entertainment industry observers believe that he will return to the post.

Mathew Littman, who leads The Working Group, which organizes Hollywood creatives, said via email, “Senator Schumer just led one of the great political wins of all time. He earned two years to lead his fellow Senate Democrats.”

A Times analysis last week showed that Schumer had the public support of 16 senators and Van Hollen had the backing of 6, with 4 more calling for change. But more than two dozen senators’ backing is unknown.

Spokespersons for Schumer and Van Hollen did not return requests for comment.

But a campaign aide to Schumer, Angelo Roefaro, told Politico that he was behind a bit of pranks-manship in advance of the release of the letter. He gained access to the Google doc draft of the letter and added Frank Sinatra’s name to the list of signatories, and subbed in Schumer’s name for Van Hollen. A Times reporter initially posted a copy of the letter endorsing Van Hollen, but with Sinatra’s name still included, before replacing it with an image of the corrected letter, per Politico. Roefaro told Politico that Schumer was unaware of the prank.

#3198. BlackStar’s Luminary Gala Returns For Fourth Edition; Mahershala Ali & Mara Brock Akil Among Honorary Award Winners

Mahershala Ali and Mara Brock Akil were among the honorary award winners at the BlackStar Projects’ Luminary Gala, which returned for its fourth edition on November 20 at The Bellevue Hotel in Philadelphia.

Cinematographer John Simmons and Stanley Nelson and Marcia Smith’s Firelight Media were also among those honored with career awards on the evening.

BlackStar Projects, the parent organization of the BlackStar Film Festival, hosts the gala, which also serves as a fundraiser for the film festival. The BlackStar Film Festival celebrated its 15th anniversary in August. Previous honorees include Mira Nair, Menelik Shabazz, Ava DuVernay, Julie Dash, Autumn Durald Arkapaw, and Wu-Tang’s RZA. Related Stories News Caron Creighton On Capturing The Fight To Save Northern California's Largest Homeless Encampment With Her Debut Feature 'Wood Street' News Haile Gerima Dissects His 10 Hour Documentary Feature 'Black Lions - Roman Wolves' & Teases His Next Project On America's Black Maroons

“It’s really incredible to be here with you at our fourth annual Luminary Gala and in the BlackStar Film Festival’s 15th year,” Maori Karmael Holmes, founder, chief executive, and artistic officer of BlackStar Projects, said as she opened the evening’s festivities. Watch on Deadline

“Back in 2012, we were all volunteers trying to put together a one-time event to celebrate the best of Black cinema from around the world. I couldn’t have imagined being here in 2026, in front of such illustrious guests, with BlackStar producing not only the festival, but also our print journal, an annual seminar at Stanford, and dozens of year-round screenings—all led by a truly brilliant staff.”

Ali, who arrived at the gala fresh off the global rollout of his latest feature, Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, also reminisced on the early iterations of the BlackStar Film Festival as he took the stage to receive his honorary award. Ali was introduced by André Holland.

“I’m moved to tears. BlackStar, Maori Holmes—thank you for having me. It’s an honor to be here,” Ali began. “I got to visit years ago, in 2014, and witness the festival in its early years. It was amazing then, so I can’t imagine what it’s like now.”

Ali continued, telling the audience that he arrived at the gala asking himself, “How did I get to a place where someone would feel I was worthy of this kind of love and honor?”

“I kept going back to my own luminaries, and one in particular: my grandmother. She’s 92, and she’s the light in my eyes. She’s like my best friend,” Ali said, before emotionally recalling how his grandmother helped instill confidence in him as a young kid growing up in Hayward, California.

“She’d have me repeat after her: I’m handsome. I’m intelligent. I can do anything I put my mind to. I can be anything I want to be,” Ali recalled.

Ali said his grandmother was also one of the first supporters of his decision to pursue acting.

“This was 30 years ago, almost to the day. I was working at a record industry magazine for minimum wage, which was about $4.50 an hour at the time. I was trying to figure out what I was doing with my life,” Ali said. “After spending the summer at the California Shakespeare Festival, I knew passionately that I wanted a shot at acting. I was auditioning for NYU, and I’d told my grandparents many times that they only accept about 18 kids from around the country, so pray for me.”

Some months before his NYU audition, Ali said, his grandmother returned from the grocery store with bundles of sweats and jumpers.

“I said, What are those for? She said, You’re going to need these when you move to New York,’ Ali recalled.

“She has been my light. I’m so grateful to my mother, of course, but my grandmother—what she’s done for me over my 50-some-odd years on this earth is guide me to have real belief in myself and my God-given talents,” he said.

“She taught me to try to be of service to others and to something larger than myself, to try to be a generous actor every day, and to want for others what I want for myself. I try to embody those things. They all come from the best grandmother in the world, Mamie Gilmore.”

Fireflight CEO Loira Limbal and Rafiah Vitalis, the company’s Senior Director of Finance and Operations, accepted the honorary award on stage for Nelson and Smith, who were also in attendance.

The company is a nonprofit organization that supports, resources, and advocates on behalf of documentary filmmakers of color. Fireflight is best known for its Documentary Lab. Accepting the honorary award, Limbal and Vitalis paid tribute to Nelson and Smith.

“26 years ago, our co-founders sat down with the simple, stubborn idea that the stories of our communities deserve to be told by filmmakers from those communities and those filmmakers deserve support, mentorship, and a place to build,” Vitalis said. “Everything we are is thanks to you two.”

Limbal and Vitalis said Fireflight was born out of a long tradition of socially conscious Black and Indigenous non-fiction filmmaking.

“Our work is to carry that tradition forward, not as a tribute or memory, but as a continuation,” Vitalis said, adding, in union with Limbal: “To every filmmaker in this room, keep holding the camera, keep framing the questions, keep the archive.”

Next up on the BlackStar calendar is the Greaves Seminar, a symposium for Black, Brown, and Indigenous film artists at Stanford. The seventh edition of the seminar takes place from March 5-7, 2027.

The 75-inch Hisense U6SF Pro has dropped to $747.97 from $1,399.99 for Black Friday sale—bringing it to its lowest price to date. The rest of the U6 Pro lineup is discounted as well, so you can pick up the same TV in sizes from 55 inches to a massive 100 inches, for anyone with the room for something closer to a home-theater-sized screen. Whichever size you choose, you’ll get free delivery to the room of choice—a service that normally costs $19.99. As for the TV itself, it’s a 2026 model that sits below the U7SG (also on sale for $1,297.99, from $1,999.99) in Hisense's lineup as the brand's entry point into Mini LED, pairing a 4K panel and local dimming with a matte, anti-reflective coating meant to cut down on glare, notes this PCMag review.

For a budget set, the U6 Pro gets a lot right when it comes to picture quality—its high peak brightness helps it hold up during a sunny afternoon in a living room with big windows, so a daytime football game or cooking show won’t look washed out, while its excellent contrast and effective local dimming keep dark scenes looking deep when you settle in for a movie at night. It also does a good job cleaning up lower-quality content, which is useful for older cable broadcasts or compressed YouTube videos—and its Fire TV interface makes it easy to jump between those kinds of content and the major streaming services without needing a separate streaming device.

The U6 Pro also brings plenty to the table for gaming, with HDMI 2.1, VRR, ALLM, and a 144Hz refresh rate that PC gamers can push to 240Hz at a lower 1080p resolution. That said, the panel’s slow response time and poor motion performance can reportedly make fast-moving scenes look noticeably blurry. Viewing angles are limited too, with the picture losing quality fairly quickly when you move off-center—and its built-in speakers aren’t particularly impressive either, so a soundbar could be worth budgeting for.

Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

#3196. Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93

IEEE also bids farewell to innovators in space, power, and telecom

Bishnu Saroop Atal received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

#3195. Apple Watch SE 3 vs Series 12: Which should you buy this holiday season?

The holiday shopping season is here, and Apple Watch is always a popular gift. Apple’s lineup includes the affordable Apple Watch SE 3 and the more advanced Apple Watch Series 12.

Here’s how those two Apple Watch models stack up…

The Apple Watch SE 3 is the most affordable way to enter the Apple Watch ecosystem. It got a big update last year, adding a variety of new higher-end Apple Watch features. It now offers an Always-On display, sleep apnea notifications, temperature sensing, interactive wrist flick and double tap gestures, and more.

The Apple Watch SE 3 offers 18 hours of battery life, though you can stretch that to 32 hours in Low Power Mode. It supports fast charging, going from 0-80% in 45 minutes.

Even though it hasn’t been updated in a year, the Apple Watch SE 3 is a very compelling option, especially for people new to the Apple Watch ecosystem. It’s pretty fantastic that you can get an Apple Watch with key display and health-monitoring features for under $200.

The Apple Watch Series 12 is Apple’s newest smartwatch, and it’s a big update over its predecessor. This year, Apple doubled down on the health and fitness capabilities of Apple Watch with an all-new Health Sensing System.

Apple touts that the Apple Watch Series 12 delivers “the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” In fact, the company conducted a study of more than 1,000 participants that found the Series 12 “achieved statistically better overall accuracy than every competing wearable it tested across workouts and daily activities.”

With the new system, Apple Watch Series 12 captures your heart rate every five seconds. Previous Apple Watch models, including the Apple Watch SE 3, take measurements every five minutes. The new Health Sensing System also enables a new readiness score feature, which factors in your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score.

As I wrote in my review, the Apple Watch Series 12 brings some of the biggest improvements to Apple Watch health tracking in years. The new sensing system unlocks a trove of new data along with better accuracy.

The Apple Watch lineup is incredibly strong right now. Whether you’re deciding between the SE 3 and Series 12, both offer great health tracking, battery life, and connectivity. The Apple Watch SE 3 is an excellent choice for people new to the Apple Watch ecosystem.

The Apple Watch Series 12, however, is the best Apple Watch for most people. There are major improvements to the health tracking capabilities, offering meaningful steps forward in what the Apple Watch can tell you about yourself. In the two months I’ve had mine, I’ve come to appreciate the more frequent heart rate measurement and readiness score.

What do you think of the current Apple Watch lineup? Are you shopping for one this holiday season? Let us know down in the comments.

Eight years ago, I bought my first Philips Hue product: the Hue Go Portable Lamp. Eight years later, the bowl-shaped, battery-powered lamp still works, and it has quite a few friends.

Philips Hue is one of the few tech ecosystems I’ve genuinely enjoyed investing in, and one that has become more valuable to me over time. But Philips Hue does have a reputation for being expensive. That's why I consider Black Friday deals one of the best opportunities to either get started with Hue or expand an existing setup.

Ahead of the shopping holiday, I asked Marco Merolla, Executive Vice President and Business Leader of Connected Lighting at Philips Hue, about the company's approach to affordability, product longevity and the future of smart lighting.

His answers shed some light on why customers like me keep coming back, and where there's still room for improvement when it comes to connected smart homes.

I'm vehemently anti-big-light. One of my proudest domestic achievements is successfully converting my fiancé to the cause, too.

My apartment is laden with lamps, most of which are from IKEA. I also have a Hue light strip running along the back of my Lovesac couch and Hue bulbs in the built-in pendant lights above my kitchen island. But generally, rather than buying smart-specific fixtures, I prefer picking out lamps that complement my mid-century modern decor and making them smart myself.

Merolla described smart lighting as a gradual progression rather than an all-at-once overhaul. Most people start with a single room or routine and build outward as they see how it fits their space. Still, I was curious how Hue reconciles its need to keep selling products with customers' expectations that their relatively expensive lights will last.

If you're just getting started with Philips Hue, this four-pack is an affordable way to turn the lamps you already own into smart lights, complete with adjustable white lighting, millions of colors and the option to expand your setup down the road.

“Our goal is not to encourage replacement for its own sake, but to give consumers meaningful reasons to expand and enhance their existing smart lighting setup as their needs change,” Merolla said.

The other side of that equation is lowering the barrier to entry without fragmenting the system. Hue's more affordable Essential range runs on the same underlying software and ecosystem connectivity as its flagship lights, trimming peak brightness and color performance to hit a friendlier price. It’s a smart option if you're outfitting an entire apartment and don't need top-tier output in every corner lamp..

I've extensively tested competing smart lighting products in varying price ranges from Govee, Wyze and Nanoleaf. Govee, in particular, makes some incredibly fun lighting fixtures, and its adoption of Matter has made it a more compelling option for Apple Home users like myself.

But I've experienced software glitches with these other brands over the years. Nearly a decade into my smart home journey, I simply don’t have patience for connected gadgets that don't work as expected 100% of the time. Sharing a home with someone less interested in technology makes reliability and simplicity even more important.

“Physical controls remain important, since not everyone wants to reach for their phone every time they adjust the lights,” Merolla said.

While you don't technically need a Bridge to get started with Hue, I'd recommend picking one up while it's on sale to unlock whole-home lighting control, advanced automations, Apple Home integration and more opportunities to expand your setup.

Despite my investment in Hue, I rarely need to open the app for everyday lighting controls. Between wall-mounted Hue dimmer switches and shortcuts I've configured in my iPhone's Control Center through Apple Home, the lights feel as immediate as traditional switches.

You don't actually need a Bridge to get started. Bluetooth-enabled Hue bulbs work directly with your phone for up to 10 lights. But upgrading to a Bridge unlocks remote access, advanced automations, Apple Home integration and entertainment synchronization, while scaling up to 50 lights and 12 accessories on the standard model.

If you're eyeing the newer Bridge Pro, you get triple the capacity, wireless placement without an Ethernet tether, and MotionAware, a feature that uses subtle signal shifts across your existing bulbs to detect movement without dedicated motion sensors.

If you're serious about building out your smart home, the Bridge Pro offers more room to expand, faster performance and MotionAware technology that can turn compatible Hue lights into motion sensors.

“The Hue Bridge continues to play an important role in delivering a robust, connected lighting experience, while innovations such as MotionAware demonstrate how lighting infrastructure can become more intelligent and responsive to people’s needs,” Merolla said.

If you're planning to expand beyond a few bulbs, I'd invest in the infrastructure now rather than revisit your setup later.

If you've already established a Hue ecosystem, the Philips Hue Play HDMI Sync Box is easily one of my favorite ways to get more out of it.

What I love about the experience is that it isn't limited to a light strip behind my TV. The lights I've already accumulated around my living space can react to what's happening on screen, making my apartment feel like one cohesive entertainment setup.

One of my absolute favorite smart home accessories, the 8K Sync Box lets you synchronize up to 10 compatible Philips Hue lights with what's happening on your TV through connected HDMI devices, making your entire living room feel like an extension of the screen.

Hue has also been finding new ways to make entertainment lighting more interesting. Earlier this year, it introduced Sports Live, which uses live soccer match data to trigger lighting effects. It doesn't even require a Sync Box if you already have a Bridge and compatible color lights.

The Sync Box is admittedly a luxury, and it wouldn't be my first Hue purchase if I were starting from scratch. But it's exactly the kind of accessory I'd wait until Black Friday to buy

As much as I appreciate Hue's reliability, I'd love to see more intelligence built into the experience. Whenever I add another lamp to my living room, for example, I have to revisit my entertainment area's lighting configuration. Smarter spatial mapping could make that process considerably easier.

The product that started my Philips Hue obsession eight years ago, this compact, bowl-shaped, battery-powered lamp is incredibly versatile for everything from setting the mood at dinner to adding a colorful accent to a bookshelf, and remains one of my favorite entry points into the Hue ecosystem.

I'm not the only one looking for refinements. In a 2026 wishlist discussion on the Philips Hue subreddit, users called for more granular brightness controls, better Natural Light scene integration with third-party platforms and the ability to group multiple bulbs in a single fixture.

Merolla told me that the company sees an opportunity to move beyond simply controlling individual devices.

“We believe the future of smart lighting is less about controlling individual devices and more about creating experiences that naturally respond to the way people live.”

If I had to rebuild my smart home tomorrow, I'd probably start exactly where I did eight years ago: with a little Hue Go or a handful of smart bulbs.

The beauty of building a smart lighting ecosystem is that you don't need to buy everything at once. And with Black Friday discounts, you can take that first step (or if you’re like me, your next one) for considerably less.

#3193. Anthropic launches new Claude Ship feature for builders

Anthropic is launching a new tool for builders called Claude Ship. The new AI feature allows Claude to “review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows.”

Claude Ship is a new product created especially for builders who code with agents. The idea is to make handling pull requests as automated as agentic coding.

“That’s why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta,” Anthropic says. “It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what’s ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person. The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.”

Claude Ship is comprised of three agents: Code Review, PR Steward, and Claude Approvals.

“Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually,” Anthropic says.

“Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the new /ship command in Claude Code,” Anthropic says.

You can learn much more about Claude Ship here. Additional documentation can be found here.

#3192. Travel Routers Turn Public Wifi Into Your Own Private Network, and This TP-Link Is Under $100 for Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

A novel solution for connecting to the internet on the go, the TP-Link Roam 7 travel router is now down to $83.49 from $119.99 for Black Friday, marking its lowest price to date. This isn't a full-size home router but, as the name suggests, a compact travel companion that measures roughly the size of a paperback book, with foldable antennas that let it slip easily into a bag.

More about convenience than chasing top speeds, you can use the Roam 7 as a standard router, connect it to public wifi to create a private network, or share your phone's internet through USB tethering. It also supports Ethernet input and USB modems, along with range extender and wireless client modes. That flexibility is particularly useful when you’re juggling a laptop, phone, and maybe a tablet and would prefer not to sign each one into a shaky network separately. Setup is straightforward through the TP-Link Tether app: scan a QR code, choose your connection type, and you’re online in a few minutes.

Once it’s running, the hardware covers the basics, with a 2.5 Gbps port for a wired connection like a hotel’s Ethernet jack, a 1 Gbps port for a wired device, and a USB 3.0 port for a storage drive or phone tethering. And since it draws power over USB-C (5V/3A), a basic power bank can keep it going through a long layover or a camping trip. As handy as it is on the road, though, it’s not meant to replace a full-size home router—even with its 5 GHz band and Wi-Fi 7 support—which will generally offer better coverage and more consistent speeds. Real-world performance also depends heavily on your connection and setup. USB tethering, for example, can feel slower than using your phone directly. It also leaves out features like automatic band steering, so you may end up managing networks yourself. Still, if you travel often or need a portable network hub for multiple devices, you’ll find it holds up pretty well.

#3190. The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry

How a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion helped shape the motors and generators that drive modern industry

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

The dynamo-electric principle: one idea, 160 years, millions of motors.

This article is brought to you by Innomotics.

In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics, a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants.

The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century.

This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions.Innomotics

The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems.

Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations.Innomotics

Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades.

Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award.

Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements.Innomotics

AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency.

For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production.

Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime.

The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance.Innomotics

What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance.

For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half.

Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running.

#3189. Apple announces Ted Lasso season 5 is coming

Apple TV (now $6.99/month for limited time) has just announced that Ted Lasso will return for season 5. Here are the details.

This summer Apple TV aired the highly anticipated return of Ted Lasso.

Season 4 debuted three full years after the last season ended, and brought a fresh start to one of the streamer’s all-time most beloved series.

But after the season 4 finale aired, Apple provided no indication whether the show would continue or not.

Now, uncertainty around the show’s fate is over.

Apple has announced that Ted Lasso season 5 is officially coming.

Following its hit fourth season, Apple’s global phenomenon “Ted Lasso” is officially returning back to the pitch for season five. Starring and executive produced by Emmy Award winner Jason Sudeikis, the fourth season of “Ted Lasso” introduced the Lady Greyhounds, with critics hailing it as “a perfect setup for a fresh return” and “one of the most beloved comedy shows of the decade.”

The announcement is light on further details. However, there should be a much shorter wait for season 5 than there was for season 4.

Before Ted Lasso returned this year, Jason Sudeikis shared that he had a new three-season arc in mind. Apple’s Eddy Cue also suggested the company would be happy to continue making more seasons for years to come.

But until today’s announcement, the lack of official news still put Lasso fans’ hopes on pause.

Whether it returns in 2027 or, perhaps more likely 2028, Ted Lasso isn’t going away again anytime soon.

Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones are 45% off right now, down to $199 for Black Friday, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet. Colors include in Dewdrop Mint, Eucalyptus Green, and Hazelnut Taupe. Weighing around 8.1 ounces, they’re among the lightest premium noise-canceling headphones, with generously padded earcups and a cushioned headband that spreads pressure without gripping too tightly, making them comfortable to wear for extended periods. They’re also easy to pack for travel, as the earcups fold and swivel for storage in the included hard-shell carrying case. The removable earpads are another welcome touch, since you can replace them as they wear down without having to retire the entire pair.

Comfort aside, noise cancellation is another area where these headphones deliver, doing a particularly good job of reducing lower-frequency rumble and background chatter, though some higher-pitched voices can still come through, notes this PCMag review. As for their sound profile, it leans warm and bass-forward, with deep lows that suit bass-heavy genres, while the companion app adds Bose Immersive Audio for spatial sound and lets you create customized listening profiles—the three-band EQ is fairly basic, though, so anyone who likes fine-tuning their sound may find the adjustment options limiting.

Connectivity, too, brings some useful upgrades over the previous generation, including Bluetooth 5.4, multipoint pairing for two devices, Google Fast Pair, and lossless audio over USB-C. That same USB-C port lets you charge the headphones while you listen, and the included USB-C-to-3.5mm cable covers standard headphone jacks, including the ones on in-flight entertainment systems. That said, battery life is less impressive, topping out at 24 hours with ANC enabled, although a 15-minute charge adds around 2.5 hours of playback. Wireless audio is also limited to the standard AAC and SBC codecs, with no support for the higher-quality aptX Adaptive—a feature available on Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra Headphones.

The trio is in the locker room, with little reveals shown in their compartments: Santos’ says The Pitt returns on a pink sticky note, and Mel finds a small package that also has a pink sticky note that reads January 7.

Offering support for iPhone and Android’s tracking networks, the new Kodak SlideTag offers the neat added functionality over an AirTag of being able to show your photos and more on an E-Ink display.

The Kodak SlideTag is inspired by classic 35mm slides from Kodak cameras, and is built by the same company, Reto, that launched a keychain digital camera inspired by old Kodak cameras too. The tracker’s E-Ink display is designed mainly to showcase your photos, with storage built-in for up to 12 photos, but also the ability to show lists and QR codes.

There are nine total styles for the SlideTag, all sold in a blind box format. You can order one tracker for $35 with the whole set also available for purchase.

Eight of the styles have a one-in-eight chance of finding, while the ninth style is only found in one out of every 64 boxes.

#3184. This Portable JBL Speaker Is a Lifehacker Gift of the Year, and It's 36% Off for Black Friday

While tech can get pretty expensive, especially in our current "RAMageddon" era, there are still plenty of affordable devices out there. The problem, of course, isn't quantity, but quality: Buying a tech item for under $50 is risky, since many of these products are made as cheaply as possible. If you're looking for a portable Bluetooth speaker, for instance, you don't want to buy something with poor sound quality, or that doesn't easily connect to your devices, or that breaks unexpectedly.

You don't need to worry about any of that with the JBL Go 4. This is a solid portable speaker that just so happens to have an MSRP of $49.95. It's so good, I named it Lifehacker's best gift under $50, as its price, excellent sound quality, and feature set make it a great option for most anyone on your list. It's an even better buy during Black Friday, too: Right now, you can pick up the JBL Go 4 for as low as $31.95, 36% off the original retail price.

JBL's Go 4 is a small speaker, but it gets surprisingly loud—especially for a speaker at this price point. Like other JBL speakers, it places a particular emphasis on bass. This is a tiny speaker, so don't expect a subwoofer on the go, but not only will it let you hear the bass in your music, it is noticeably punchy. JBL advertises seven hours of playtime on a single charge here, which is often plenty for taking the speaker out and about for the day. You can net an additional two hours of if you engage "Playtime Boost." JBL doesn't specify how this works, but it likely cuts some of the frequencies here to save on battery life. And, since it's 1P67-rated against dust and water, it's a great choice for outdoor use.

Perhaps my favorite thing about the JBL Go 4 is that it supports Auracast. That means you can easily connect to any other Auracast-compatible JBL speaker using the Auracast button on each device. I've used this before at parties and gatherings for an impromptu multi-speaker setup. Since JBL is so popular, it's not impractical to assume one or two other people at the function might have a similar speaker you can connect to, or if you know friends or family members have JBL speakers of their own, you can coordinate these setups ahead of time.

This discount is only available on specific colors of the Go 4, at least on Amazon: Black, White, Blue, Purple, Red, and "Squad." Black and Orange, Pink, and Sand are all still $49.95. Again, the JBL Go 4 is absolutely worth the $50 MSRP, but unless you're married to one of those three colors, it's even better at a discount.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

The best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). #3181. Doc Talk Podcast: ‘The Eyes Of Ghana’s Ben Proudfoot & Nana Frimpong On Their Oscar Contender Backed By The Obamas & IShowSpeed

Director Ben Proudfoot’s Oscar-contending documentary The Eyes of Ghana has attracted some impressive supporters, including former occupants of the White House.

Former President Barack Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama are among the executive producers of the nonfiction feature through their Higher Ground production company. How could you possibly top that? Well, in addition to the Obamas, The Eyes of Ghana has gained the backing of Darren Watkins Jr, better known to his fans as IShowSpeed, who, according to some measures, is the most popular livestreamer on the planet. In fact, Speed is about to release the film for free on his YouTube channel.

Two-time Oscar winner Proudfoot and producer Nana Frimpong join the latest edition of Deadline’s Doc Talk podcast to discuss their film, which is vying to make the Motion Picture Academy’s nonfiction feature shortlist (voting for that begins December 7). The documentary tells the story of a remarkable man named Chris Hesse, now in his 90s, who served as the personal cinematographer to Ghana’s first president, Kwame Nkrumah. In that role, Hesse captured extraordinary footage of the pan-Africanist leader who showed the way for many other countries on the continent to shed their colonial rulers and emerge into independence.

Hesse’s invaluable archive was thought to have been lost forever, but Proudfoot and team discovered otherwise. The director and his producer explain the unlikely course of events that revealed the existence of the precious materials in a London hideaway. They also tell us how Barack and Michelle Obama came on board, and how they connected with YouTuber Speed.

Proudfoot also shares how he enlisted his friend Kris Bowers, his co-director on the Oscar-winning The Last Repair Shop, to compose the score for The Eyes of Ghana and where they recorded the music — at a place closely associated with The Beatles.

RELATED: Kris Bowers On Creating A Love Letter To Ghana & Film History With His Score For ‘The Eyes Of Ghana’ – Sound & Screen Film

That’s on the new episode of Doc Talk hosted by Oscar winner John Ridley (12 Years a Slave, Shirley), and Matt Carey, Deadline’s senior documentary editor. The pod is a production of Deadline and Ridley’s Nō Studios.

#3178. Veruschka Dies: German Supermodel Of The 1960s & ’70s Who Appeared In ‘Blow-Up’ Was 87

Veruschka, the German supermodel of the 1960s and ’70s who appeared in Michelangelo Antonioni’s iconic Swinging London film Blow-Up and was christened by photographer Richard Avedon as “the most beautiful woman in the world,” has died. She was 87.

Her death was announced by Germany newspaper Bild. A cause of death has not been disclosed, but Bild reports that she died surrounded by friends and family at her home in Berlin. Various media reports indicate November 24 as the date of her death.

Born Vera Gottliebe Anna Gräfin von Lehndorff-Steinort into German aristocracy on May 14, 1939, in Königsberg, East Prussia, Germany, Veruschka was only 5 when, according to Vogue magazine, her father, Count Heinrich von Lehndorff-Steinort, was executed following a failed 1944 plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler.

By age 20, Veruschka had moved to Florence, where she began modeling after meeting photographer Ugo Mulas. Within a couple years she had adopted the Russian-sounding name Veruschka, a moniker befitting her statuesque frame and stark, even severe beauty. By the mid-1960s she had moved to New York, was modeling for the Ford Modeling Agency and on her way to becoming what was considered Germany’s first supermodel. She was a favorite of the era’s leading photographers including Avedon, David Bailey and Irving Penn.

A brief appearance in Antonioni’s 1966 Blow-Up furthered her status in a fashion world dominated by such British models as Twiggy and Jean Shrimpton, and she would soon make the covers of Vogue, Life and other major publications of the day.

Veruschka largely retired from the fashion world by the mid-1970s, often citing a regime change at Vogue as a cause. She said in a 2009 interview that the magazine’s new editor Grace Mirabella “wanted me to be bourgeois, and I didn’t want to be that. I didn’t model for a long time after that.”

Although she only occasionally returned to modeling over the decades, Veruschka remained an iconic signifier of glamorous fashion, such as when she appeared in 2006’s Casino Royale as a poker player sharing a table with Daniel Craig’s James Bond.

Information on survivors was not immediately available.

#3177. iOS 27.2 upgraded Apple Photos in two ways, here’s what’s new

Apple Photos got a lot of new features in iOS 27, but the recent release of iOS 27.2 brought even more improvements. Here’s what’s new.

Shared Albums are among my favorite features in the Photos app. I don’t post on social media often, but I love using Shared Albums because they provide a social media-style experience in a private way that lives right inside Photos.

iOS 27 brought a variety of big improvements to Shared Albums. And in iOS 27.2, Apple introduced four more.

Per Apple’s release notes, here’s what’s new:

To get these new features, you’ll need to make sure your Shared Albums have been upgraded for iOS 27.

One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated.

This challenge extends to AI-edited photos too, which might have key details changed by tools like iOS 27’s Extend, Reframe, and Clean Up features in Photos.

Apple is tackling the issue with its new Reference Image feature in iPhone 18 Pro, and also through a software enhancement that rolled out in iOS 27.2.

Per Apple, its latest software update adds the following:

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground

SynthID is a cross-platform standard developed by Google that embeds unnoticeable digital watermarks into AI-modified photos. Users won’t see a visible watermark, but anyone who checks for a SynthID marker will find it.

#3174. NFL On The Future Of Netflix’s Thanksgiving Eve Game & Starting A New Tradition: “We Are Committed”

Netflix is launching a new annual NFL tradition: the first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game. The inaugural game will see the Los Angeles Rams and the Green Bay Packers face off a day before the Thanksgiving Day tripleheader, giving fans more football to enjoy with friends and family during the holiday season.

Grace Senko, NFL Vice President, Media Strategy and Business Development, recently told Deadline how this special game came to be.

“As part of our scheduling process every year, the team takes a look at the upcoming year and looks at potential windows and thinks about how we can continue to innovate the schedule, try new things that we’ve never done before,” Senko said. “[Last year] when we played Christmas on a Wednesday, that was the first time, and then now it’s become kind of a staple throughout the season.”

She continued, “When we think about Thanksgiving Eve, I don’t think we think about Thanksgiving as just being one day. At least I know it feels like everybody in New York has already left a little bit. But for a lot of people, it begins on that Wednesday, already gathering with friends and family, and that kind of extends through Sunday.” Watch on Deadline

Senko notes that the Thanksgiving Day games “continued to perform really strong and really well” last year, adding that they averaged 45M viewers “and was the fourth consecutive year of viewership growth.”

“When you see that, and then you pair that with the Black Friday game that Amazon began distributing in 2023, and the really strong growth over the last few years there, it really made us question: you know, should we be doing something on Thanksgiving Eve? Is there a special moment that we can create there as well, and really, you know, continue to kind of build and expand upon the temple that we’ve already established with Thanksgiving Day?” she added.

Senko says that the game is “an extension of the Thanksgiving Day holiday” and “a unique opportunity that we had in our schedule,” adding, “We are committed to play on Thanksgiving Eve through the duration of our deal with Netflix.”

The Thanksgiving Eve Halftime show will feature U2 amid their 50th anniversary celebration tour. Senko goes back to the Christmas Day game in 2024, which was dubbed Beyoncé Bowl as the singer performed during Halftime, adding, “I think Netflix, at kind of the core of entertainment and culture in our country, is focused on making it as big of a possible moment and event as they possibly can.

Netflix is set to bring the Thanksgiving Eve game back in 2027 as part of their deal with the NFL. This game could potentially be the start of a new tradition for many decades to come.

“We’ll look at this year, but then over time we’ll look at the audience growth,” Senko said about the future of the Thanksgiving Eve game. “We’ll look at feedback from our partners. We’ll get feedback from the clubs, feedback from the various constituents in the organization, and evaluate if it’s a day and an event that we want to continue building. So that’s definitely there. There’s a lot of conversations that will be had, but a lot of different things that we’ll look at, whether evaluating this game or any other window that we’re playing in. That’s kind of new and a non-traditional window, I would say.”

Netflix’s Thanksgiving Eve game streams on Wednesday, November 25, starting at 8 p.m. ET / 5 p.m. PT and will feature U2 during the halftime show.
